head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Set comprehension: every node that is the target of some edge (has an incoming edge)
[i for i in range(n) if i not in has_in]
Sources of a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)

p: A node with no incoming edge cannot be reached from any other node, so it must be in the set. Every other node has a predecessor, and following predecessors backwards in an acyclic graph must end at a node with no incoming edge, so the sources reach everything.

1557.takeaway: In a DAG, the nodes with no incoming edge are the smallest set that reaches everything.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: sorted((dist, i, j) for i < j)
Every pair of points as an edge with Manhattan distance, sorted by weight
Kruskal's algorithm needs the edges sorted
Union-Find (disjoint set): the group root of x
Edge joins two different components: safe to take
A spanning tree has n − 1 edges; stop early

p: 5 points. Edges accepted in sorted order (rejected edges, which would close cycles, are skipped):

blocks.h: Why does sorted greedy give the cheapest connection?
p: Kruskal's algorithm repeatedly adds the cheapest edge that does not create a cycle. By the cut property, the cheapest edge crossing any split of the points belongs to some minimum spanning tree, so each greedy choice is safe.

bullets: Time: O(n² log n): about n²/2 edges sorted.
Space: O(n²) for the edge list. Prim's algorithm with a heap avoids storing all edges.

1584.takeaway: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree: sort all pair distances and union-find to skip cycles.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: XOR (exclusive or) the running answer with the current number
Shift right: moves to the next higher-order prefix of the bits
XOR of n, n>>1, n>>2, … equals the position of n in the Gray code sequence
Converting a Gray code to its rank

p: `n = 6` (binary 110):

blocks.h: Why is this the Gray code inverse?
p: The operation sequence in the problem (flip the last bit, or flip the bit left of the lowest set bit) walks through the Gray code. The step count to reach 0 from n is the index of n in that sequence. The index is computed by `n ^ (n >> 1) ^ (n >> 2) ^ …`, the standard Gray-to-binary conversion, so it is simply XOR-ing the shifted values.

1611.takeaway: The minimum operations equal the Gray-to-binary conversion n ^ (n>>1) ^ (n>>2) ^ …

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Cells grouped by value; values are processed from smallest to largest
Process in increasing order so smaller ranks are final
The largest rank assigned so far in each row and column
Within a group of equal values, cells sharing a row or column must get the SAME rank, so they are merged (column j is node m + j, to keep row and column ids apart)
Merging equal cells connected by a row or a column
The rank for a connected group is 1 + the largest earlier rank in any of its rows and columns
update row_max / col_max after the group
Only after all of the group's ranks are known, so cells in the same group don't affect each other early

p: `[[1,2],[3,4]]`: values handled in increasing order (answer matrix, row maxima, column maxima after each group):
bullets: Final: `[[1, 2], [2, 3]]`. A matrix with all equal values `[[7, 7], [7, 7]]` gives `[[1, 1], [1, 1]]`: all cells are connected, so they share one rank.

blocks.h: Why union equal cells in the same row or column?
p: Equal values in one row or column must have the same rank (the rank rule says they cannot differ), and that equality chains: if A shares a row with B and B shares a column with C, then A, B and C all get one rank. Union-Find finds those groups, and each group takes 1 plus the maximum prior rank over all its rows and columns.

bullets: Time: O(m·n log(m·n)) for sorting, plus near-constant Union-Find operations.

1632.takeaway: Process values ascending; equal cells linked by a row or column share a rank = 1 + the largest rank already placed in their rows/columns.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Post-order DFS (Depth-First Search): what each subtree found
node is p or node is q
Identity match with a target node; counts it and returns it
node if l and r else (l or r)
If both sides found a target, this node is the LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor); otherwise pass up whatever was found
Both targets must exist in the tree; this problem allows a missing node, so a count is needed
Difference from Lowest Common Ancestor I

bullets: Targets found: 2, so the LCA is node 5. With `q` absent from the tree the search finds only 1 target and returns `None`.

p: Without it, if q is missing the recursion would return p (the only target found), which looks like an LCA but is wrong. The counter confirms both nodes were actually seen. Because the search does not stop at the first match (it keeps going into both children), q is still found when it lies below p.

1644.takeaway: LCA that counts how many targets were found, so a missing node returns None.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Handle the largest frequency first so it keeps its value if free
Another letter already has this frequency
Delete one occurrence to lower the frequency by one
Marks the final frequency (a frequency of 0 means all copies deleted, which is always allowed)

p: `"aaabbbcc"` has frequencies 3, 3, 2:

Only deletions are allowed. Each letter's count can only go down, and the cheapest way to make counts distinct is to move each to the largest still-free value not above it. Processing from the biggest ensures that values are claimed in the best order.

bullets: Time: O(n + K²) where K is the number of distinct letters (≤ 26).

1647.takeaway: Greedy: from the largest frequency down, decrement until it is unused or zero.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Two pointers, one from each node, climbing the parent links
Same trick as intersection of two linked lists
a = a.parent if a else q
When a pointer runs off the top, it restarts at the OTHER starting node, which equalizes the path lengths
Stops when both pointers sit on the same node (identity)
Their meeting point is the lowest common ancestor

blocks.h: Why do the pointers meet at the LCA?
p: The node paths are a-to-root and b-to-root. After a pointer finishes its own path (length x + c, where c is the common part above the LCA) it continues on the other node's path. Both pointers have then walked the same total length, x + y + c, so they arrive at the LCA together (or both fall off the top together if there is none).

bullets: Space: O(1), unlike the set-of-ancestors approach (O(h)).

1650.takeaway: Two parent pointers that swap starting nodes after falling off the top meet at the LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The last n cells in row-major order, each 0 (empty), 1 (introvert) or 2 (extrovert); this is the 'profile' of the boundary
The neighbour above is the oldest digit (the one about to leave the profile); the neighbour to the left is the newest digit (none at the start of a row)
Drops the up digit and makes room for the new cell's digit
Introvert: 120 alone, −30 per neighbour; extrovert: 40 alone, +20 per neighbour. `pair[a][b]` is the combined effect on both cells (−60, −10 or +40)
Pre-computing the happiness change per neighbouring pair
Leave empty, place an introvert, or place an extrovert (if any remain)
Memoizes states (position, profile, introverts left, extroverts left)

p: `m = 2`, `n = 3`, 1 introvert, 2 extroverts. The best arrangement, found by the memoized search over 3^(n−1) profiles, gives total happiness:
bullets: The pair table reflects interactions: two extroverts next to each other add 40 (20 each), two introverts subtract 60, and an introvert next to an extrovert subtracts 10 (−30 for the introvert, +20 for the extrovert).

blocks.h: Why only the last n cells in the state?
p: A cell interacts only with the cell above and the cell to the left. Processing in row-major order, the cells that can still matter for future placements are exactly the last n cells, so the profile is n digits (and since the oldest leaves each step, 3^(n−1) distinct states plus one new digit).

bullets: Space: the same order for the cache; n ≤ 5 keeps it small.

1659.takeaway: Broken-profile DP: scan cells in order, keep the last n cells in base 3, add each placement's gain from the up/left neighbours.

What it does

String equality: same characters in the same order

bullets: Both become `abc`, so the answer is True, even though the pieces are split differently.

p: Joining uses O(total length) extra memory. If memory mattered, two index pointers (word index, character index) walking both lists in parallel would compare character by character in O(1) extra space, and stop at the first mismatch.

bullets: Space: O(total length) for the joined strings.

1662.takeaway: Join each list and compare; two-pointer streaming is the O(1)-space alternative.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Order by actual − minimum, the most negative (largest gap between minimum and actual) first
Total energy supplied at the start
if cur < minimum: need += minimum - cur
Top up just enough to meet the task's minimum requirement

p: After doing a task you lose `actual` but needed `minimum`; the unused buffer `minimum − actual` stays unspent. Doing the tasks with the biggest buffer first keeps leftover energy high for later tasks (an exchange argument shows swapping two adjacent tasks out of this order never reduces the required start energy).

bullets: Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

1665.takeaway: Sort by (actual − minimum) ascending and top up energy lazily when a task's minimum is not met.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A trie (prefix tree) built from nested dicts: each key is a character, each value is the child dict
Inserts every suffix of s; every substring is a prefix of some suffix
if ch not in node: node[ch] = {}; cnt += 1
A new trie node means a substring never seen before, so count it
Counting distinct strings by new nodes

p: `"aabbaba"`: inserting each suffix creates new trie nodes only for substrings not seen before:

blocks.h: Why do trie nodes equal distinct substrings?
p: Each path from the root spells a distinct string, and each trie node corresponds to exactly one such path. Because all suffixes are inserted, the set of paths is the set of all substrings, so the node count is the number of distinct substrings.

bullets: Time: O(n²), since the total suffix length is n(n+1)/2.
Space: O(n²) nodes in the worst case. A suffix automaton or suffix array reaches O(n) or O(n log n).

1698.takeaway: Insert all suffixes into a trie; each newly created node is a new distinct substring.

What it does

rows: The time the chef becomes free
The chef starts at arrival if idle, or after finishing the previous order
True division: the average as a float

p: If the chef is idle when the customer arrives (t < arrive), cooking starts at arrival; if the chef is still busy (t > arrive), it starts when the chef frees up. The maximum covers both cases.

1701.takeaway: Simulate a single chef: start = max(free time, arrival); wait = finish − arrival.

What it does
Reach for it when

Load as many of this type as fit
Stop when the truck is full

p: Every box takes one slot, so the value per slot is just its units. Filling slots with the highest-value boxes first can't be beaten: swapping a chosen low-value box for an unchosen high-value one would increase the total.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

1710.takeaway: Greedy: sort by units per box descending and fill the truck.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Neighbour sets for each node (the 'ancestor-or-descendant' relation from the pairs)
Candidates for parents come before their descendants (an ancestor is related to all its descendants, so it has at least as many neighbours)
The root must be related to every other node
Among the neighbours with degree at least d, the one with the smallest degree is the node's parent
Every neighbour of the node must also be an ancestor or descendant of its parent; otherwise no tree fits
Parent and child with equal degree can swap places: more than one valid tree

p: Pairs `[[1,2],[2,3],[1,3]]` (every node is related to every other):
bullets: Answer 2: all three nodes are related to each other, so either of the two equal-degree choices gives a valid tree. For `[[1,2],[2,3]]` (node 2 is the unique root) the answer is 1; for `[[1,2],[2,3],[2,4],[1,5]]` (5 is related to 1 but not to 2, the root) it is 0.

p: In a rooted tree, a node's neighbours in this relation are exactly its ancestors and descendants. An ancestor has all of its descendants as neighbours, so its degree is at least as large as theirs. Sorting by degree puts ancestors before descendants, so each node's parent is found among the neighbours of larger or equal degree.

bullets: Time: O(n · d) roughly, over each node's neighbours.

1719.takeaway: Sort by degree: each node's parent is its smallest-degree neighbour with degree ≥ its own; equal degrees give two answers.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Returns the lowest common ancestor of the nodes with values p and q (assuming both exist), by post-order search
LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor) in a binary tree
A target found: return it upward
n if l and r else l or r
Both sides found a target → this node is the LCA; otherwise pass up the one that was found
Distance from the LCA down to the target; `max(…)` picks the side where the target was found (the other side returns −1)
Distance between p and q = path up from p to the LCA plus down to q

p: In a tree there is exactly one path between two nodes, and it goes up to their lowest common ancestor and then down. Its length is the sum of the two vertical distances. If one node is the ancestor of the other, the LCA is that node and its depth is 0, giving just the other depth.

1740.takeaway: Distance = depth(p below LCA) + depth(q below LCA).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Adjacency lists: each pair says two numbers are neighbours in the array
Only the two ends of the array have one neighbour; all others have two
Finding the endpoint of a path
nxt = g[cur][0] if g[cur][0] != prev else g[cur][1]
Step to the neighbour that is not the one we came from
Either end works (the problem accepts either direction); `min` makes the result deterministic

blocks.h: Why is the graph a simple path?
p: The array has n distinct values and n−1 adjacent pairs, and each interior value appears in exactly two pairs. The graph is therefore a path, and walking it from an endpoint rebuilds the array.

1743.takeaway: Build an adjacency graph, start at a value with one neighbour, and walk the path.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The next index, wrapping from the last element to the first (circular comparison)
Treating the array as a circle
A sorted array, rotated, has at most one drop (the rotation point)

blocks.h: Why compare the last element to the first?
p: A non-decreasing array has no drop on the circle except possibly the wrap from last to first. Rotating it moves that one drop to the rotation point. If the array was not sorted, at least two drops appear when going around the circle.

1752.takeaway: Count drops around the circular array (including last→first); a rotated sorted array has at most one.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Compares each digit with the pattern 0101…, where position i should be i % 2
Changes to reach '1010…': exactly the other positions
Pick the cheaper of the two alternating patterns

p: `"0100"` compared with the pattern `0101`:
bullets: diff = 1 to reach 0101; to reach 1010 it takes 3. Answer 1.

blocks.h: Why is `len(s) - diff` the cost of the other pattern?
p: The two alternating patterns differ at every position, so a position that matches one pattern mismatches the other. The number of mismatches with the second pattern is therefore the number of matches with the first, len(s) − diff.

1758.takeaway: Count mismatches against 0101…; the other pattern costs n minus that.
